title: Yeti: The Asian Bigfoot
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Yeti, the legendary ape-like creature of the Himalayas and Tibetan plateau, often called the Asian Bigfoot. They cover Sherpa folk tales (including the Annihilation of the Yeti story), the 1921 journalist Henry Newman's "abominable snowman" translation, Charles Howard-Bury's expedition, the 1951 Eric Shipton footprint photo, Anthony Wooldridge's rock photo, Edmund Hillary's scalp and the Jimmy Stewart smuggled finger, Tom Slick's hunting expeditions, DNA testing by Brian Sykes and Bryan Sykes-era analysis showing bears, Reinhold Messner's views, Soviet/Russian Yeti tourism hoaxes, and Gigantopithecus. The episode closes with a listener mail about Cole's Custard and the Wendy's finger story.

segments.title: Cryptozoology banter and what the Yeti is
segments.summary: Hosts banter about past cryptozoology episodes, then describe the two versions of the Yeti: a huge eight-foot creature and a smaller wild hippie-like being in the Himalayas.

segments.title: Sherpa folklore and the Annihilation of the Yeti
segments.summary: Sherpa tales collected by Shiva Kumar in Folk Tales of Sherpa and Yeti share a cautionary moral like Grimm's fairy tales. The Annihilation of the Yeti story involves Sherpas getting Yetis drunk so they fight, with one killed by a lama. Alexander the Great is said to have asked about seeing a Yeti.

segments.title: Abominable snowman origin and early sightings
segments.summary: Journalist Henry Newman reported British explorers' footprint findings and mistranslated the Sherpa term mito kangmi as abominable snowman. Howard-Bury led the expedition. A 1925 description from two hikers, recorded by Mira Shackley, described a reddish-haired, roughly eight-foot creature.

segments.title: Eric Shipton footprint and Daniel Taylor's Barun Valley
segments.summary: Eric Shipton's 1951 photo of a crisp, large, oddly shaped footprint became world famous. Daniel Taylor later searched the Barun Valley in Nepal, found no Yeti, and helped turn it into a protected area. He suggested a tree bear might have made the track, though the valley's climate makes that unlikely at high altitude.

segments.title: Melting tracks, Wooldridge photo, and Ernest films
segments.summary: Benjamin Radford's skeptical point that sun-melted snow tracks can look alien. Anthony Wooldridge's photo of supposed Yetis turned out to be rock outcroppings. Hosts joke about the Ernest films.

segments.title: Hillary's scalp, Jimmy Stewart's finger, and Tom Slick
segments.summary: Edmund Hillary brought back a supposed Yeti scalp from a Nepal monastery, later identified as serow. Jimmy Stewart helped smuggle a supposed Yeti finger out of India; DNA later showed it was human. Tom Slick, a hunter, was banned from killing Yetis, then changed to a non-lethal search, especially for Bigfoot.

segments.title: DNA testing of Yeti samples
segments.summary: Brian Sykes at Oxford collected 57 samples in 2000 and analyzed 36. A few were initially linked to a Pleistocene polar bear, but reanalysis showed brown bears. Reinhold Messner's sample turned out to be a dog tooth, and he came to believe they were all bears.

segments.title: Russian Yeti hoaxes, Gigantopithecus, and closing
segments.summary: Russian Yeti claims in Siberia, including branch beds that appear man-made, are linked to tourism promotion. Putin reportedly claimed to see three Yetis from a helicopter in 2016. Gigantopithecus is mentioned as a possible basis for the legend, and the hosts conclude that bears are the likely explanation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Cole's Custard and the Wendy's finger
segments.summary: Listener Ethan Lyons writes that Cole's Custard in North Carolina was mentioned in the Wendy's chili episode as a place a finger was found, and says he has been there often.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
